lead: Every emission control is a choice of place: stop the pollutant forming inside the cylinder, or convert and trap it in the exhaust. In-cylinder methods change mixing, timing and temperature. After-treatment adds catalysts, filters and urea. A petrol engine held at stoichiometric mixture can use one three-way catalyst; a lean diesel needs an oxidation catalyst, a particulate filter and SCR or a NOx trap. The skill is matching each device to the engine’s air–fuel ratio and exhaust temperature.
prereq: You need: how CO, HC, NOx and PM form (formation of CO, HC and NOx, smoke and particulate matter).

blocks.text: In-cylinder methods cut what the engine makes in the first place:

items: Spark or injection retard: the burn moves later, the peak temperature falls and NOx falls. It costs fuel; in a diesel it raises PM.

Injection strategy (CI): higher pressure (common rail) gives finer sprays and less soot; a pilot injection shortens the delay and softens the first burst, lowering noise and NOx; a post injection late in expansion burns soot or supplies heat for the filter; rate shaping starts the injection slowly.

Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR): exhaust sent back to the intake replaces some oxygen and adds CO2 and H2O, which absorb heat. The flame runs cooler, so NOx falls. Cooled EGR packs more mass into the cylinder; high-pressure EGR is taken before the turbine, low-pressure EGR after the particulate filter. Too much EGR raises PM, HC and fuel use.
Air–fuel control (SI): an oxygen (lambda) sensor and closed-loop injection hold λ = 1 for the catalyst.
Chamber and charge motion: a compact chamber with fewer crevices cuts HC; swirl and squish speed mixing and cut soot.
Crankcase ventilation and evaporative control: blow-by gas is sent back to the intake, and fuel vapour from the tank is held in a charcoal canister and burnt later.

blocks.text: EGR % = (CO₂ intake − CO₂ ambient) ÷ (CO₂ exhaust − CO₂ ambient) × 100
blocks.where: each CO₂ is a volume (mole) per cent on the same basis; the result is the share of exhaust in the intake charge.

sections.h3: After-treatment: the three-way catalyst and the diesel line

blocks.text: The three-way catalyst (TWC) is a ceramic honeycomb coated with platinum, palladium and rhodium. At λ = 1 it does three jobs at once: CO + ½O2 → CO2; HC + O2 → CO2 + H2O; and NO is reduced by CO, H2 and HC, for example 2NO + 2CO → N2 + 2CO2. The reductions need the CO and HC that the oxidations use up, so the window is narrow: λ within about ±0.5 % of 1, roughly an air–fuel ratio of 14.6 to 14.8. Lean of it, spare oxygen takes the reductants and NOx passes; rich of it, CO and HC pass. A catalyst works only above its light-off temperature, about 250 to 300 °C, so most of a cycle’s emissions come in the first minute.
A diesel’s exhaust always holds spare oxygen, so it needs a different line:

items: Diesel oxidation catalyst (DOC): burns CO, HC and part of the SOF, and turns some NO into NO2, which helps the next two devices.

Diesel particulate filter (DPF): a wall-flow honeycomb whose channels are blocked at alternate ends, so the gas must pass through the porous walls and the soot stays behind. It is cleaned by regeneration: passively by NO2 at about 250 to 400 °C, or actively by raising the gas to about 600 °C with a post injection. Ash cannot burn and slowly fills the filter.

Selective catalytic reduction (SCR): a 32.5 % urea solution (AdBlue) is sprayed into the exhaust and breaks down to ammonia: (NH2)2CO + H2O → 2NH3 + CO2. The standard reaction is 4NH3 + 4NO + O2 → 4N2 + 6H2O, one ammonia per NO; the fast reaction uses equal NO and NO2. Unused ammonia (ammonia slip) is burnt in a small slip catalyst at the end.

Lean NOx trap (LNT): stores NO2 as barium nitrate while lean; a short rich pulse every minute or so releases it and reduces it to N2. It needs no urea but is poisoned by sulphur and costs fuel for the rich pulses.

blocks.text: The diesel order is fixed by chemistry: the DOC first, because it makes NO<sub>2</sub> for passive regeneration and for fast SCR; the DPF next, so the SCR is not fouled by soot; urea after the DPF so the ammonia is not burnt during regeneration; the slip catalyst last. Fuel sulphur must be low (10 ppm in BS-VI fuel), since sulphur poisons the DOC, LNT and SCR and adds sulphate PM.

examples.question: An EGR valve opens on a diesel engine. CO<sub>2</sub> is 0.04 % in the ambient air, 1.80 % in the intake manifold and 12.0 % in the exhaust. Find the EGR rate as a share of the intake charge, and the mass of exhaust recirculated per kg of fresh air.
steps: Rise of CO<sub>2</sub> in the intake caused by EGR: 1.80 − 0.04 = 1.76 %.
Rise it would have if the whole charge were exhaust: 12.0 − 0.04 = 11.96 %.
EGR share x = 1.76 ÷ 11.96 = 0.147, that is 14.7 % of the intake charge.
Fresh air is the rest: 1 − 0.147 = 0.853 of the charge.
Exhaust per kg of fresh air: x ÷ (1 − x) = 0.147 ÷ 0.853 = 0.173 kg.
examples.answer: EGR is 14.7 % of the intake charge, which is 0.173 kg of exhaust per kg of fresh air (taking mole and mass fractions as equal, since the molar masses of air and diesel exhaust are close).

examples.question: A 200 kW truck diesel makes 6.0 g/kWh of engine-out NOx (as NO<sub>2</sub>). The SCR must remove 90 % of it. Find the urea and AdBlue flow at full load and compare the AdBlue with the diesel flow at a brake specific fuel consumption of 210 g/kWh.
steps: Standard SCR uses one NH<sub>3</sub> per NO, so 23.5 mol/h of NH<sub>3</sub>.
Each urea molecule gives two NH<sub>3</sub>: urea = 23.5 ÷ 2 = 11.7 mol/h; × 60.06 g/mol = 705 g/h.
AdBlue is 32.5 % urea: 705 ÷ 0.325 = 2169 g/h, about 2.17 kg/h.
Diesel flow: 210 × 200 = 42 000 g/h = 42 kg/h; AdBlue ÷ diesel = 2.17 ÷ 42 = 0.052.
examples.answer: The engine needs about 0.70 kg/h of urea, that is 2.17 kg/h of AdBlue, about 5 % of its diesel flow, and the tailpipe NOx falls to 0.6 g/kWh.

traps: Fitting a three-way catalyst alone to a lean engine. With spare oxygen the NO reduction stops, so NOx passes unconverted.
Giving the TWC window as “λ ± 0.3”. That spans air–fuel ratios from about 10 to 19; the real window is about ±0.5 % of λ = 1.

Dividing by (CO<sub>2</sub> exhaust − CO<sub>2</sub> intake) and calling the answer the EGR share of the charge. That ratio is exhaust per unit of fresh air (17.3 % in the example), not the share of the charge (14.7 %).
Mixing up DOC and DPF: the DOC oxidises gases, the DPF traps solid soot.
Saying regeneration empties the filter. It burns soot; ash stays.

quiz.q: Write the three reactions of a three-way catalyst.
quiz.a: CO + ½O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub>; HC + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O; 2NO + 2CO → N<sub>2</sub> + 2CO<sub>2</sub> (NO is also reduced by H<sub>2</sub> and HC).

quiz.q: What is ammonia slip, and how is it handled?
quiz.a: Ammonia that leaves the SCR unreacted. A small oxidation (slip) catalyst after the SCR burns it.

quiz.q: Why does EGR lower NOx but raise PM?
quiz.a: EGR replaces oxygen with CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O, which absorb heat, so the flame is cooler and has less oxygen: less NO forms. The same lower temperature and oxygen slow soot burn-out, so PM rises.

quiz.q: Why is the DOC placed before the DPF and the SCR?
quiz.a: It turns NO into NO<sub>2</sub>, which burns soot in the DPF at low temperature and speeds up SCR through the fast reaction; it also removes CO and HC first.

quiz.q: CO<sub>2</sub> is 0.04 % ambient, 1.50 % in the intake and 10.0 % in the exhaust. Find the EGR share of the charge.
How much urea and water are in 10 kg of AdBlue?
A three-way catalyst is fitted to a lean-burn petrol engine running at λ = 1.4. Which gases are converted and which are not? Suggest a fix.
quiz.a: CO and HC are oxidised, since oxygen is plentiful. NOx is not reduced, because the spare oxygen consumes the CO, H<sub>2</sub> and HC that would reduce it. A lean NOx trap with short rich purges, or urea SCR, is needed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cold start now dominates tailpipe emissions, so makers place catalysts close to the exhaust manifold, add electrically heated catalysts, and run mild hybrids that warm the catalyst before the engine fires. Trucks use NOx sensors before and after the SCR to set the urea dose and detect a faulty system, which then limits engine torque. Search next for “close-coupled SCR”, “electrically heated catalyst” and “DPF regeneration strategy”.
